sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Goroutines and channels are Go's primary differentiator for concurrent backend services — they let you write thousands of concurrent operations without threads or callback hell. The Go scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads, so spawning 100k goroutines is routine and cheap. Every meaningful Go backend question eventually lands here: HTTP handlers, background workers, streaming pipelines, and graceful shutdown all require fluency with this model. Interviewers use this topic to separate candidates who have read Go from those who have shipped Go.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: A goroutine is a green thread managed by the Go runtime — it starts at 2KB of stack (grows as needed up to 1GB by default) and is scheduled cooperatively at I/O and function call points. A channel is a typed, thread-safe pipe: `ch := make(chan int)` creates an unbuffered channel where every send blocks until a receiver is ready and vice versa. A buffered channel `make(chan int, 10)` allows up to 10 items in flight before the sender blocks. Closing a channel signals receivers that no more values are coming — receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately with the second `ok` boolean set to false.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Goroutine lifecycle**: launched with `go f()`, no handle returned; goroutines are not garbage collected if they block — you must ensure they can exit.
- **Buffered vs unbuffered channels**: unbuffered = synchronous handoff; buffered = async up to capacity.
- **Channel direction types**: `chan<- T` (send-only) and `<-chan T` (receive-only) in function signatures enforce one-way use and are a common API pattern.
- **Closing channels**: only the sender should close; closing a nil channel panics; sending to a closed channel panics.
- **Goroutine leaks**: a goroutine blocked on a channel with no remaining senders/receivers leaks forever — the #1 source of memory leaks in Go services.
- **Fan-out/fan-in**: fan-out distributes work across N goroutines each reading the same input channel; fan-in merges N result channels into one using a multiplexer goroutine.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Goroutine leak patterns**: HTTP handler spawns goroutine that blocks on a channel — request completes but goroutine lives forever; fix with context cancellation.
- **Send to closed channel**: panics at runtime — there is no safe way to send to a channel after close; design so only the producer closes.
- **Receive from closed channel**: returns `(zero-value, false)` immediately; `range ch` exits cleanly when the channel is closed.
- **Range over unclosed channel**: `for v := range ch` blocks forever waiting for more values if the channel is never closed — a common trap in pipeline code.
- **nil channel**: sending or receiving on a nil channel blocks forever; select ignores nil channels — a useful pattern for dynamically disabling cases.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Goroutines are the unit of concurrency in Go — they're managed by the runtime scheduler, start at about 2KB of stack, and you can have hundreds of thousands running without the overhead of OS threads. Channels are how goroutines communicate safely: an unbuffered channel forces a synchronous handoff, while a buffered channel lets you decouple producers and consumers up to the buffer size. One thing I always watch for is goroutine leaks — if a goroutine is blocked on a channel and there's no way to unblock it, it lives forever and leaks memory. I prevent this by threading a context through my goroutines so they can exit on cancellation, and I always make sure only the sender closes a channel to avoid panics."
